Request → Offer → Discover → Acknowledge (RODA)
Acknowledge → Offer → Discover → Request (AODR)
Offer → Discover → Request → Acknowledge (ODRA)

explanation: The DHCP lease process (DORA): 1) DHCPDISCOVER: the client (no IP yet) broadcasts to 255.255.255.255, destination port UDP 67 (DHCP server). Asks: 'Is there a DHCP server? I need an IP address.' 2) DHCPOFFER: one or more DHCP servers unicast or broadcast a response offering an available IP address along with subnet mask, lease duration, and options. Source port UDP 67, destination port UDP 68 (DHCP client). 3) DHCPREQUEST: the client broadcasts which offer it accepts (typically the first received). Also used for lease renewal. Informs other servers their offer was not chosen. 4) DHCPACK: the chosen server acknowledges the assignment. The client can now use the IP address. DHCP lease renewal: at 50% of the lease time, the client unicasts a DHCPREQUEST to renew with the original server. At 87.5%, it broadcasts a DHCPREQUEST if the first renewal failed. DHCP options: Option 1 (subnet mask), Option 3 (default gateway/router), Option 6 (DNS servers), Option 51 (lease time), Option 66 (TFTP server), Option 150 (TFTP server for Cisco phones).

prompt: A network team needs a centralized authentication system for network administrators logging into routers and switches. The system must support per-command authorization so different admin levels can run different commands. Which protocol best supports this?

options.text: RADIUS — combines authentication and authorization, encrypts the entire packet
TACACS+ — separates authentication, authorization, and accounting and supports per-command authorization on network devices
LDAP — provides directory lookups but no device authorization
Kerberos — designed for workstation authentication, not network device CLI access

explanation: RADIUS vs TACACS+ comparison: RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service): UDP ports 1812 (authentication) and 1813 (accounting). Combines authentication and authorization in one exchange. Encrypts only the password field in the packet. Better suited for network access (VPN, wireless 802.1X, dial-up). Supported by most devices and vendors. TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus): Cisco-proprietary (though widely supported). TCP port 49. Fully encrypts the entire packet body. Separates AAA — Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting into independent processes. Supports per-command authorization — different admin users can be authorized to run specific commands on specific devices. Provides detailed accounting of every command executed. Best for network device administration (router/switch management). For network device administration with granular per-command authorization: TACACS+ is the answer. For 802.1X wireless or VPN user authentication: RADIUS is typically used. Many enterprises use both: RADIUS for user network access, TACACS+ for network device administration.

prompt: A company wants to ensure that only authenticated, compliant devices can connect to the wired network. When a device plugs into a switch port, it should be forced to authenticate before gaining any network access. Which technology enforces this?

options.text: Port security — limits connections by MAC address
802.1X (NAC) — the switch blocks all traffic except authentication until the device successfully authenticates via a RADIUS server
STP — controls which ports forward traffic
VLANs — separate traffic but do not authenticate devices

explanation: 802.1X is a port-based Network Access Control (NAC) standard that requires devices to authenticate before network access is granted. Components: Supplicant: the device/software on the endpoint requesting access (Windows has a built-in 802.1X supplicant). Authenticator: the switch (or wireless AP) that enforces access — blocks all traffic except EAP authentication frames until the device authenticates. Authentication Server: a RADIUS server (e.g., Microsoft NPS, FreeRADIUS) that validates credentials. Process: device connects to switch port → switch blocks traffic → sends EAP-Request to device → device provides credentials (certificate, username/password) → RADIUS validates → switch receives Access-Accept → port is opened. Authentication methods (EAP types): EAP-TLS: certificate-based (most secure). PEAP: username/password wrapped in TLS tunnel. EAP-FAST: Cisco's flexible method. After authentication: the RADIUS server can send VLAN assignment attributes — placing the device in the appropriate VLAN based on identity or device type. Failed auth: device is placed in a guest VLAN or denied.

prompt: An organization connects to two different ISPs for redundancy. The network engineer needs a routing protocol that can advertise the company's public IP address space to both ISPs and intelligently control which ISP's path inbound traffic uses. Which routing protocol is required?

options.text: OSPF — the best interior gateway protocol for large networks
EIGRP — Cisco's advanced distance-vector protocol
BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) — the only exterior gateway protocol used on the internet
RIP — simple distance-vector protocol using hop count

explanation: BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the routing protocol of the internet — the only EGP (Exterior Gateway Protocol) in widespread use. It routes traffic between autonomous systems (AS), where each ISP and large organization has a unique AS number (ASN). Why BGP for dual-ISP connections: Advertise the organization's public IP prefix to both ISPs so traffic can arrive via either path. Control inbound traffic using BGP path attributes (AS Path prepending, Local Preference, MED). Control outbound traffic using local preference on which ISP to prefer for different destinations. Automatic failover: if one ISP's BGP session drops, traffic automatically routes through the other. BGP characteristics: TCP port 179. Path-vector protocol — decisions based on AS path attributes, not just metric. Very slow convergence compared to OSPF/EIGRP. Highly configurable with many attributes for traffic engineering. OSPF, EIGRP, and RIP are interior gateway protocols (IGPs) used within a single organization's network — they cannot exchange routing information between different organizations' networks on the internet.

prompt: A small branch office router needs to send all internet-bound traffic to its ISP gateway at 10.0.0.1. Which routing configuration accomplishes this with the least administrative effort?

options.text: Configure OSPF between the branch router and the ISP router
Add a static default route: ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 10.0.0.1
Configure BGP to learn all internet routes
Enable RIP on all interfaces and wait for route convergence

explanation: A static default route (also called the gateway of last resort) tells the router: 'For any destination not in my routing table, forward the packet to 10.0.0.1.' Syntax: ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 [next-hop-IP or exit-interface]. The 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 matches any destination address and any subnet mask — the most general possible route (administrative distance typically 1 for static). This is the simplest and most common configuration for a small office with a single exit point. When to use static routes: small networks with predictable traffic patterns, stub networks with only one path out, specific network destinations that should always use a fixed path. Dynamic routing protocols (OSPF, BGP, EIGRP): automatically learn and update routes — used in larger networks with multiple paths where automatic convergence is needed. A static default route is nearly always used at branch/small office sites connecting to a single ISP — minimal configuration, no overhead, reliable.

prompt: A network engineer replaces an old hub with a managed switch. Which specific problem does this replacement solve?

options.text: The hub caused routing loops — switches prevent loops with STP
The hub sent all traffic to all ports (collision domain), causing congestion — the switch forwards traffic only to the intended destination port
The hub could not support VLANs — switches support VLANs natively
The hub used coaxial cable — the switch supports twisted pair

explanation: Hub vs switch: Hub (Layer 1 — Physical): sends every received frame out all ports except the incoming port. All devices share a single collision domain — only one device can transmit at a time. Collisions are frequent as the number of devices grows. No intelligence — cannot learn MAC addresses. Operates at half-duplex. Causes excessive network congestion. Switch (Layer 2 — Data Link): learns MAC addresses by observing source addresses on each port (builds CAM table). Forwards frames only to the specific port where the destination MAC was last seen. Each port is its own collision domain — eliminates inter-device collisions. Supports full-duplex operation — simultaneous send and receive. Supports VLANs, port security, QoS, spanning tree, and many other advanced features. Result of replacing hub with switch: dramatically reduces collisions and unnecessary traffic, each port gets dedicated bandwidth, full-duplex support doubles effective link speed. Hub still creates one broadcast domain — so does a switch (broadcasts still reach all ports in the same VLAN).

prompt: A security audit finds that SNMP v2c is in use across all network infrastructure. The auditor recommends upgrading to SNMP v3. What specific security capabilities does SNMPv3 add?

options.text: SNMPv3 uses TCP instead of UDP for more reliable delivery
SNMPv3 adds authentication (verifies message source) and encryption (AES/DES) — SNMPv1 and v2c transmit community strings in cleartext
SNMPv3 supports more MIB objects than v2c
SNMPv3 eliminates the need for a management server

explanation: SNMP version comparison: SNMPv1: introduced in 1988. Uses community strings (like passwords) sent in cleartext. GET, SET, TRAP operations. No authentication or encryption. SNMPv2c: added BULK operations (more efficient retrieval) and 64-bit counters for high-speed interfaces. Still uses plaintext community strings. No security improvement over v1. SNMPv3: added three security levels: noAuthNoPriv: no authentication, no encryption (like v2c). authNoPriv: HMAC-MD5 or HMAC-SHA authentication — verifies message integrity and source. authPriv: authentication + DES or AES encryption — protects data in transit from eavesdropping. Uses USM (User-based Security Model) with user accounts instead of community strings. Provides access control (VACM — View-based Access Control Model). Highly recommended for any production network. SNMPv1/v2c community strings: 'public' (read-only) and 'private' (read-write) are default values that should always be changed — but even with changed values, they travel in cleartext and can be captured by wireshark.

prompt: A network monitoring system receives a syslog message with severity level 0. What does this indicate and how should the NOC team respond?

options.text: Level 0 is informational — no action needed
Level 0 is Emergency (system is unusable) — the highest severity, requiring immediate response
Level 0 means the message was filtered and is not a real alert
Level 0 is a debug message — lowest priority

explanation: Syslog severity levels (RFC 5424): 0 — Emergency: system is unusable. Immediate action required. Examples: kernel panic, complete power failure. 1 — Alert: action must be taken immediately. Examples: database corruption, full disk on critical system. 2 — Critical: critical conditions. Examples: hardware failure, software crashes. 3 — Error: error conditions that should be investigated. 4 — Warning: warning conditions — potential problems. 5 — Notice: normal but significant conditions worth noting. 6 — Informational: informational messages (routine events). 7 — Debug: debug-level messages — extremely verbose, used only during troubleshooting. Memory aid: Every Awful Crisis Erodes Wonderful Network Infrastructure Daily (Emergency, Alert, Critical, Error, Warning, Notice, Informational, Debug). Syslog configuration: devices send messages to a syslog server (port UDP 514 or TCP 6514 for TLS). The 'logging trap' level command on Cisco devices sets which severity levels are sent. SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) systems aggregate and correlate syslog messages from multiple sources.

prompt: During a VoIP quality assessment, users report calls sounding 'choppy' with audio cutting in and out, even though there is no significant packet loss. Which network metric most directly causes choppy audio in VoIP?

options.text: High latency — one-way delay above 150ms
High jitter — variable delay between packet arrivals causing irregular audio playback
Low bandwidth — insufficient capacity for voice streams
High TTL values — packets are expiring before reaching the destination

explanation: VoIP quality metrics: Latency (one-way delay): the time for a packet to travel from sender to receiver. VoIP tolerance: under 150ms one-way (ITU G.114 recommendation). Effect: delays in conversation, talking over each other. Jitter: variation in packet arrival times (delay variance). VoIP tolerance: under 30ms. Cause of 'choppy' audio — even if every packet arrives, irregular timing causes the audio codec to play some frames too early or late, creating gaps or overlaps. Fix: jitter buffer at the receiver (buffers packets and smooths delivery); QoS to prioritize voice packets. Packet loss: lost voice packets cause audible gaps and clicks. VoIP tolerance: under 1-3%. Bandwidth: a G.711 voice call uses ~80 kbps bidirectional including headers. Modern codecs (G.729) use less. Insufficient bandwidth causes congestion leading to loss and jitter. Fix for jitter: implement QoS with priority queuing for DSCP EF (Expedited Forwarding) traffic; reduce jitter buffer delay for better interactivity versus stability tradeoff.

prompt: A network engineer wants to upgrade the firmware on a core switch during business hours. Company policy requires approval before any changes to production infrastructure. What process must be followed?

options.text: Proceed immediately — firmware updates are always safe
Submit a change request through the change management process, including a rollback plan, and obtain approval from the Change Advisory Board (CAB) before proceeding
Only get approval for major changes — firmware is a minor update
Notify the team via email and proceed after 15 minutes if no objection

explanation: Change management is a formal process to control modifications to IT infrastructure and minimize unplanned outages. Key components: Change request: document what is changing, why, the risk level, implementation steps, and a rollback plan. Change types: Standard (pre-approved routine changes), Normal (requires CAB review), Emergency (urgent, streamlined approval process). CAB (Change Advisory Board): reviews and approves or rejects normal change requests. Includes representatives from IT, security, and business stakeholders. Change window: schedule changes during maintenance windows (typically low-usage periods, not business hours). Rollback plan: documented steps to undo the change if something goes wrong — essential for any production change. Post-implementation review: after the change, verify it worked as expected and document results. Why during business hours is problematic: maximum user impact if the change causes an outage. Even firmware updates can fail and require reboots. Best practice: schedule firmware upgrades for maintenance windows (nights, weekends) with a maintenance notification to stakeholders.

prompt: A company's DR plan states an RPO of 4 hours and an RTO of 8 hours for its order processing system. What do these values mean?

options.text: RPO: the system must recover within 4 hours; RTO: no more than 8 hours of data can be lost
RPO: no more than 4 hours of data can be lost (backup frequency); RTO: the system must be fully restored within 8 hours of a disaster
RPO: 4-hour backup retention; RTO: 8 systems must recover simultaneously
RPO: Recovery Point Office, 4 locations; RTO: Recovery Time Office, 8 teams

explanation: Two fundamental DR metrics: RPO (Recovery Point Objective): the maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time. How old can your most recent backup be when disaster strikes? RPO of 4 hours: backups must occur at least every 4 hours. If a disaster occurs just before a backup, you lose at most 4 hours of data. Drives backup frequency and replication strategy. RTO (Recovery Time Objective): the maximum acceptable time to restore a system to operation after a disaster. RTO of 8 hours: from the moment disaster is declared, the system must be fully operational within 8 hours. Drives recovery infrastructure (hot standby vs. cold standby, automation). Relationship: lower RPO/RTO = higher cost. Near-zero RPO/RTO requires synchronous replication and hot standby systems. Hot site: fully operational parallel environment — near-zero RTO. Warm site: partially configured, needs data restoration — hours RTO. Cold site: empty facility, build from scratch — days/weeks RTO. Cloud DR (DRaaS): rapidly provision resources from cloud when needed — variable RTO based on provisioning and restore speed.

prompt: A network security analyst needs to capture and analyze all traffic flowing through a switch without disrupting normal network operations. What switch feature should be configured?

options.text: Port security — limits MAC addresses on a port
SPAN (Switched Port Analyzer) — mirrors traffic from monitored ports to a dedicated analyzer port
NetFlow — exports flow statistics to a collector
SNMP — sends device status information to a management server

explanation: SPAN (Switched Port Analyzer), also known as port mirroring: copies traffic from one or more source ports (or VLANs) to a destination port where a packet analyzer (Wireshark, IDS/IPS sensor, or network TAP) is connected. Source: one or more switch ports, a VLAN, or an EtherChannel. Destination: one dedicated port connected to the analyzer (the analyzer is not a normal network participant on this port — it only receives). Traffic direction: can mirror ingress (received), egress (sent), or both. RSPAN (Remote SPAN): mirrors traffic across the network to an analyzer on a different switch (uses a VLAN to carry mirrored traffic). ERSPAN (Encapsulated Remote SPAN): encapsulates mirrored traffic in GRE for transport across Layer 3 networks. Use cases: network troubleshooting (capture specific traffic), IDS/IPS inline or passive monitoring, application performance monitoring. NetFlow: summarizes traffic by flow (source/destination IP, port, protocol) and exports statistics — useful for bandwidth analysis and anomaly detection but not for full packet capture. A physical TAP (Test Access Point) is a hardware alternative to SPAN that passively copies physical signals.

prompt: A network uses RADIUS to control who can connect to the corporate wireless network, what resources they can access after connecting, and maintains logs of all connection activity for compliance audits. Which framework does this describe?

options.text: CIA Triad (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability)
AAA (Authentication, Authorization, Accounting)
DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) architecture
PKI (Public Key Infrastructure)

explanation: The AAA framework provides three distinct security functions: Authentication: verifying the identity of a user or device. 'Who are you?' Methods: username/password, certificate, biometric, MFA. For wireless: 802.1X sends credentials to a RADIUS server for verification. Authorization: determining what an authenticated user is allowed to do. 'What are you allowed to access?' After authentication, the RADIUS server sends attributes (VLAN assignment, ACL, time restrictions) to the switch/AP. Controls access to network resources, device commands (TACACS+), or applications. Accounting: recording what the authenticated user did and when. 'What did you do?' Logs: session start/stop times, data transferred, commands executed, resources accessed. Used for compliance audits, billing, security forensics. AAA servers: RADIUS: UDP 1812/1813, combines AuthN and AuthZ, widely supported. TACACS+: TCP 49, separates all three AAA functions, full packet encryption, preferred for network device admin. Both work with 802.1X for network access control.

prompt: An attacker connects to an access switch port and sends crafted 802.1Q-tagged frames to gain access to a VLAN they are not authorized to access. What attack is this, and what is the primary defense?

options.text: ARP spoofing — defended by Dynamic ARP Inspection
VLAN hopping via switch spoofing or double tagging — defended by disabling DTP on access ports and changing the native VLAN to an unused ID
MAC flooding — defended by enabling port security
STP manipulation — defended by enabling BPDU Guard

explanation: VLAN hopping attacks have two methods: Method 1 — Switch Spoofing: an attacker configures their NIC to send DTP (Dynamic Trunking Protocol) negotiation frames, tricking the switch into establishing a trunk link with the attacker's port. The attacker then sends traffic tagged for any VLAN. Defense: explicitly configure all non-trunk ports as access ports (switchport mode access) and disable DTP (switchport nonegotiate). Method 2 — Double Tagging: attacker sends frames with two 802.1Q tags. The outer tag matches the native VLAN (removed by the first switch). The inner tag targets the victim VLAN (processed by the next switch). Defense: change the native VLAN to an unused VLAN ID that carries no traffic (e.g., VLAN 999). Also configure all switch ports with explicit access mode. Best practices to prevent VLAN hopping: disable DTP on all access ports. Change native VLAN to an unused ID. Explicitly configure trunk ports. Disable unused ports and place them in an unused VLAN. Do not use VLAN 1 for any user traffic.

prompt: An attacker floods a network switch with thousands of DHCP DISCOVER packets using spoofed MAC addresses, exhausting the DHCP server's address pool. New legitimate clients cannot obtain IP addresses. What attack is this and what switch feature prevents it?

options.text: ARP poisoning — prevented by Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI)
DHCP starvation — prevented by DHCP snooping, which rate-limits DHCP traffic on untrusted ports
MAC flooding — prevented by port security
SYN flood — prevented by TCP SYN cookies on the DHCP server

explanation: DHCP starvation attack: the attacker uses a tool (like Gobbler or DHCPstarv) to send thousands of DHCPDISCOVER frames with different spoofed MAC addresses. The DHCP server assigns an IP to each fake MAC, exhausting the pool. Legitimate clients receive DHCPNAK or no response and get APIPA addresses (169.254.x.x). This is often combined with setting up a rogue DHCP server to hand out malicious gateway/DNS settings to clients (DHCP poisoning). DHCP Snooping (switch feature): designates trusted ports (uplinks to legitimate DHCP servers) and untrusted ports (end-device ports). Untrusted ports: DHCP server replies (DHCPOFFER, DHCPACK) are blocked — prevents rogue DHCP servers. DHCP DISCOVER and REQUEST rate are limited — prevents starvation floods. Builds a DHCP snooping binding table (IP, MAC, VLAN, port) used by Dynamic ARP Inspection. Trusted ports: all DHCP traffic is forwarded normally. DHCP snooping is a critical switch security feature that should be enabled on all access switches. DAI (Dynamic ARP Inspection) uses the DHCP snooping table to validate ARP packets.

prompt: An attacker sends millions of TCP SYN packets to a web server using spoofed source IP addresses but never completes the three-way handshake. The server's connection table fills up and legitimate users cannot connect. What attack is this?

options.text: Ping flood — ICMP-based DDoS attack
SYN flood — a TCP-based DoS attack that exhausts the server's half-open connection table
UDP flood — fills bandwidth with UDP packets
Smurf attack — ICMP broadcast amplification

explanation: SYN flood (TCP state exhaustion): exploits the TCP three-way handshake. Normal handshake: client SYN → server SYN-ACK → client ACK. Attack: attacker sends millions of SYN packets from spoofed source IPs. Server sends SYN-ACK to each spoofed IP (which never responds). Server keeps each half-open connection in the SYN queue waiting for the final ACK. Queue fills up → server cannot accept new connections from legitimate users. Defenses: SYN Cookies: the server generates a cryptographic cookie in the SYN-ACK rather than allocating state. Only allocates full connection when the final ACK arrives with the correct cookie. Prevents queue exhaustion. Firewall SYN rate limiting: limit incoming SYN packets per source IP. Load balancer / reverse proxy: absorbs SYN floods before they reach the server. Upstream scrubbing (DDoS mitigation service): ISP or CDN filters flood traffic before it reaches the network. Modern OSes have SYN cookie support enabled by default. This attack is distinct from a DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) which uses many compromised hosts — a single-source version is a DoS.

prompt: An attacker successfully inserts a fraudulent DNS record into a resolver's cache, redirecting users who query for bankofamerica.com to a malicious IP address. What attack is this and what technology prevents it?

options.text: ARP poisoning — prevented by Dynamic ARP Inspection
DNS cache poisoning — prevented by DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions) which adds digital signatures to DNS records
BGP hijacking — prevented by RPKI
SSL stripping — prevented by HSTS headers

explanation: DNS cache poisoning (DNS spoofing): an attacker injects fraudulent DNS responses into a recursive resolver's cache. When users query that resolver for the poisoned domain, they receive the attacker's IP instead of the legitimate address — redirecting them to a phishing or malware site. Attack methods: Kaminsky attack (2008): exploits the predictable 16-bit transaction ID in DNS queries to race against legitimate responses and win cache injection. Birthday attack: exploits probability theory to guess matching transaction IDs. Defenses: DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions): adds cryptographic digital signatures to DNS records. Resolvers verify signatures using the domain's public key. A poisoned record without a valid signature is rejected. Does NOT encrypt DNS, only provides authentication/integrity. Randomized source ports (port randomization): makes transaction ID guessing harder. DNS over HTTPS (DoH) and DNS over TLS (DoT): encrypt DNS traffic to prevent interception and tampering. Response Rate Limiting (RRL) on DNS servers: prevents amplification attacks.

prompt: A coffee shop customer connects to a Wi-Fi network named 'CoffeeShop_Free'. An attacker nearby has created a rogue AP with the same SSID and a stronger signal. The customer's device automatically connects to the attacker's AP. What attack is this?

options.text: War driving — the attacker is scanning for open networks
Evil twin attack — a rogue AP mimics a legitimate SSID to intercept traffic
Bluejacking — Bluetooth-based device attack
WPS brute force — exploiting the Wi-Fi Protected Setup PIN

explanation: Evil twin attack: the attacker creates a rogue access point that broadcasts the same SSID as a legitimate network. When the rogue AP has a stronger signal than the legitimate one, devices with 'auto-connect' enabled may preferentially connect to the attacker's AP. Once connected: the attacker can intercept all unencrypted HTTP traffic. Perform SSL stripping to downgrade HTTPS to HTTP. Inject malicious content into web pages. Capture credentials from unprotected login forms. Execute man-in-the-middle attacks against all traffic. Defenses: Use a VPN when on any public Wi-Fi — encrypts all traffic regardless of AP legitimacy. Verify you're on a captive portal page or ask staff for the exact network name. Disable auto-connect to open/untrusted networks. Use certificate-based wireless authentication (WPA2/3-Enterprise with 802.1X) — the server certificate verification prevents connecting to rogue APs. Look for HTTPS on all sensitive sites. Evil twin differs from a rogue AP (an unauthorized AP on the corporate network that provides unauthorized access) — though both are security threats.

prompt: A security team wants to deploy a system that not only detects malicious network traffic but also automatically blocks attacks in real time without requiring manual intervention. Which system provides this capability?

options.text: IDS (Intrusion Detection System) — detects and alerts but does not block
IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) — detects AND actively blocks malicious traffic inline
SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) — correlates and alerts across multiple sources
Firewall — only filters traffic based on static port and IP rules

explanation: IDS vs IPS: IDS (Intrusion Detection System): passive monitoring — sits out-of-band (not in the traffic path). Analyzes copies of traffic (via SPAN port or network TAP). Detects known attack signatures and anomalous behavior. Generates alerts for security analysts to investigate. Cannot block traffic — only detects. False positive: generates an alert on legitimate traffic. False negative: misses an actual attack. IPS (Intrusion Prevention System): active, inline — sits in the traffic path (all traffic passes through it). Detects AND blocks malicious traffic automatically. Can drop packets, reset connections, and quarantine hosts. Requires careful tuning — a misconfigured IPS can block legitimate traffic. Higher risk if it fails (fail-open vs fail-closed). NGFW (Next-Generation Firewall): often includes IPS functionality. Signature-based detection: matches known attack patterns. Anomaly-based detection: identifies deviations from a baseline (detects zero-days). Behavior-based detection: monitors process behavior. For automatic blocking: IPS is the answer. For monitoring without risk of blocking legitimate traffic: IDS is preferred. Most modern deployments use NGFW with integrated IPS in inline mode.

prompt: A security team deploys a server that mimics a vulnerable database server. The server has no legitimate users and should never receive normal traffic. Its purpose is to detect unauthorized access attempts and gather intelligence on attacker techniques. What is this system called?

options.text: Bastion host — a hardened server exposed to the internet
Honeypot — a decoy system designed to attract and monitor attackers
Proxy server — forwards requests on behalf of clients
Jump server — an administrative access gateway

explanation: A honeypot is a deliberately configured decoy system designed to attract attackers and gather threat intelligence without putting real systems at risk. Characteristics: Appears valuable to attackers (fake databases, file servers, credential stores). Contains no real data or legitimate users — any traffic to it is inherently suspicious. Heavily monitored — every connection, command, and action is logged. Low false-positive rate — any interaction signals a real threat. Types: Low-interaction honeypot: simulates limited services — easier to deploy, lower risk, less data. High-interaction honeypot: full real operating system — more data, higher risk if attacker escapes the honeypot. Honeynet: a network of honeypots simulating a full environment. Honeypot uses: Detect internal reconnaissance (lateral movement). Identify zero-day exploits being used. Slow down attackers (honeypots create uncertainty about which systems are real). Gather malware samples. Study attacker TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures). Legal considerations: actively redirecting real internet traffic to a honeypot (entrapment) can create legal issues — consult legal counsel. Internal honeypots are generally straightforward.

prompt: A router ACL is configured with these rules in order: (1) Permit TCP from 10.1.0.0/24 to any port 80, (2) Deny TCP from 10.1.0.0/24 to any port 443, (3) Permit IP from any to any. A host at 10.1.0.50 tries to connect to a web server on port 443. What happens?

options.text: The connection is permitted because rule 3 allows all IP traffic
The connection is denied by rule 2 before reaching rule 3
The connection is permitted because rule 1 allows HTTP from that subnet
The ACL is invalid because permit and deny cannot be mixed

explanation: ACL (Access Control List) processing rules: ACLs are processed sequentially from top to bottom. The first matching rule is applied and processing STOPS — subsequent rules are never evaluated. The packet from 10.1.0.50 to port 443: Rule 1: Permit TCP from 10.1.0.0/24 to any port 80 — does NOT match (port 443 ≠ port 80). Rule 2: Deny TCP from 10.1.0.0/24 to any port 443 — MATCHES. Packet is DENIED. Rule 3 is never reached. Key ACL concepts: Implicit deny: at the end of every ACL is an invisible 'deny all' rule. Any traffic not matched by an explicit permit is denied. Order matters: more specific rules should come before more general rules. Standard ACL: filters only by source IP. Extended ACL: filters by source IP, destination IP, protocol, and port — much more granular. ACL placement: extended ACLs should be placed close to the source. Standard ACLs close to the destination. Direction: ACLs applied to an interface in the 'in' direction filter incoming traffic; 'out' direction filters outgoing traffic.

prompt: A company adopts a Zero Trust security model. Which statement BEST describes the core principle of Zero Trust?

options.text: Trust all internal network traffic — only verify external connections
Never trust, always verify — every user, device, and connection must authenticate and be authorized regardless of network location
Trust devices that pass perimeter firewall inspection
Only users with VPN connections are trusted

explanation: Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA) is a security model that eliminates the concept of an implicit trusted zone. Traditional perimeter security assumed: 'If you're inside the network, you're trusted.' Zero Trust assumes: 'The network is always hostile — trust nothing, verify everything.' Core principles: Verify explicitly: authenticate and authorize every request using all available data (identity, device health, location, service/resource, data classification). Use least privilege access: limit user access with Just-In-Time (JIT) and Just-Enough-Access (JEA) policies — minimize the blast radius of a breach. Assume breach: design assuming attackers are already inside. Minimize blast radius, segment networks, encrypt all traffic, use analytics to detect anomalies. Zero Trust components: Strong identity (MFA, conditional access). Device health verification (MDM compliance). Micro-segmentation (limit lateral movement). Continuous monitoring and validation. Application access based on identity, not network location. Why Zero Trust: traditional perimeter security fails when: credentials are stolen, insiders are malicious, cloud and remote work dissolve the perimeter. Relevant frameworks: NIST SP 800-207, Microsoft Zero Trust model, Google BeyondCorp.

prompt: A company is upgrading its wireless infrastructure from WPA2-Personal to WPA3-Personal. What specific security improvement does WPA3-Personal provide over WPA2-Personal?

options.text: WPA3 uses AES-256 while WPA2 uses AES-128 — stronger encryption
WPA3 uses SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) instead of PSK — preventing offline dictionary attacks against captured handshakes
WPA3 eliminates the need for a wireless password entirely
WPA3 supports 2.4 GHz only while WPA2 works on 5 GHz

explanation: WPA3-Personal improvements over WPA2-Personal: SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals), also known as Dragonfly: replaces PSK (Pre-Shared Key) handshake. In WPA2-PSK: an attacker captures the 4-way handshake and performs offline dictionary attacks against the PSK. With a common password, this is highly effective. In WPA3-SAE: the authentication uses a zero-knowledge proof based on the Diffie-Hellman key exchange. An attacker cannot perform offline attacks — each guess requires an online interaction with the AP. Forward Secrecy: SAE generates a unique session key for each connection. Even if the password is later compromised, past sessions cannot be decrypted. OWE (Opportunistic Wireless Encryption): WPA3 adds encryption to open (password-free) networks. WPA3-Enterprise: uses CNSA (192-bit mode) for government/high-security environments. WPA2 still uses AES-128 (CCMP), which is not broken — the PSK vulnerability is the key issue. WPA3 transition mode: allows WPA2 and WPA3 clients to coexist during migration.

prompt: A technician follows CompTIA's network troubleshooting methodology. After gathering information and identifying a probable cause, what is the NEXT step?

options.text: Document findings and close the ticket
Escalate to senior staff immediately
Test the theory to determine the cause — verify whether the probable cause is actually responsible for the problem
Implement the solution and notify the user

explanation: CompTIA's 7-step network troubleshooting methodology: 1. Identify the problem: gather information, question users, identify symptoms, research recent changes. 2. Establish a theory of probable cause: consider multiple possibilities using OSI model (bottom-up, top-down, divide and conquer). 3. Test the theory: run tests to confirm or disprove the theory. If confirmed, move to step 4. If disproved, go back to step 2 and form a new theory. 4. Establish a plan of action: identify how to resolve the problem with minimal impact; consider escalation. 5. Implement the solution or escalate: make the change; follow change management if required. 6. Verify full system functionality: confirm the issue is resolved for all affected users; implement any preventive measures. 7. Document findings, actions, and outcomes: create a knowledge base entry; close the ticket. The key distinction: testing the theory (step 3) must happen before implementing a solution (step 5). Jumping straight to a fix without testing the theory risks making changes that don't solve the actual problem.

prompt: A newly installed Cat6 cable passes a wire map test but users on that run experience intermittent connectivity drops and reduced speed. A cable certifier shows high NEXT (Near-End Crosstalk) values. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The cable is too long — exceeds 100-meter limit
The cable has excessive untwisting of wire pairs near the termination point (more than 0.5 inches), causing signal interference between pairs
The cable is connected to the wrong switch port
The switch port is configured for the wrong VLAN

explanation: Crosstalk is electromagnetic interference between adjacent wire pairs within a cable. Types: NEXT (Near-End Crosstalk): interference measured at the transmitting end — the transmit signal 'leaks' into adjacent pairs at the near end. FEXT (Far-End Crosstalk): interference measured at the receiving end. PS-NEXT (Power Sum NEXT): crosstalk from all pairs combined. Most common cause of high NEXT: excessive untwisting of wire pairs at termination. Cat5e allows maximum 1/2 inch (13mm) of untwisting. Cat6 requires even tighter: maximum 3/8 inch (10mm). More untwisting = more signal leakage between pairs = higher crosstalk = slower speeds and errors. Other crosstalk causes: poor quality connectors or crimping, incorrect wiring pinouts, cable damage. Cable certification tools (Fluke DTX, JDSU): measure NEXT, FEXT, attenuation, delay skew, and other parameters against TIA/EIA standards. Pass/fail per category specification. Solution: re-terminate both ends of the cable, minimizing untwisting. If the cable itself is damaged internally, replace it.

prompt: A cable run tests at 115 meters using a cable certifier. Users on this run experience slow performance and frequent disconnects. The cable is Cat5e. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The cable exceeds the 100-meter maximum length for Ethernet — signal attenuation is too high for reliable communication
The cable has a split pair wiring error
The cable is connected to an incorrect VLAN on the switch
The switch needs a firmware update to support longer cable runs

explanation: Attenuation is the loss of signal strength as it travels through a cable. Ethernet specifications: Maximum cable run length for 1000BASE-T (Gigabit Ethernet) over Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6a: 100 meters (328 feet) from switch port to device, including patch cables at both ends. The 100-meter limit comes from the maximum attenuation allowed before the signal degrades too much for reliable reception. At 115 meters, the run exceeds the specification by 15 meters, causing: Excessive signal attenuation — the receiving device struggles to distinguish 1s and 0s. Increased error rates — the switch and NIC negotiate down to lower speeds (100 Mbps, then 10 Mbps) to maintain reliability. Intermittent disconnects when environmental factors (temperature, EMI) make conditions worse. Solutions: Re-route the cable to be within 100 meters. Install a switch (Layer 2 device) midway to extend the run — each switch-to-device segment gets its own 100-meter budget. Use fiber optic cable — supports much longer distances with negligible attenuation. Install a media converter to transition from copper to fiber for the long run.

prompt: A user's laptop connects to the corporate 802.1X wireless network successfully at their desk but cannot connect from the conference room — they receive an 'Authentication failed' error. Other users in the conference room connect fine. What is the MOST likely cause specific to this user?

options.text: The conference room AP is offline
The user's client certificate has expired or is not present, causing 802.1X authentication to fail
The conference room is on a different SSID than the main office
The conference room has too many connected clients

explanation: 802.1X uses EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) for authentication. Common EAP methods: EAP-TLS: requires a client certificate on the device — the most common enterprise method. PEAP: username and password wrapped in TLS (no client cert required). EAP-FAST: Cisco method. For EAP-TLS specifically, authentication fails if: The client certificate has expired. The certificate was issued by a CA not trusted by the RADIUS server. The certificate was removed from the device (disk wipe, re-image, policy change). The device's computer account certificate expired (machine authentication). The RADIUS server's certificate is not trusted by the client. Since other users in the same conference room connect fine: the AP and RADIUS server are working. The issue is specific to this user's device configuration, most likely an expired or missing certificate. Resolution: check certificate validity in the Certificate Manager on the client device. Re-enroll the certificate through Group Policy (for domain-joined devices: gpupdate /force). Check the RADIUS server logs for the specific rejection reason — it will identify the exact EAP failure code.

prompt: A technician runs 'ping 8.8.8.8' and gets replies but 'ping google.com' fails with 'Request timeout.' What is the most likely problem and how is it diagnosed?

options.text: The default gateway is incorrectly configured
DNS resolution is failing — the device can reach the internet by IP but cannot resolve hostnames to IPs
The firewall is blocking ICMP traffic
Google's servers are down

explanation: This is a classic DNS failure symptom: IP connectivity works (ping to 8.8.8.8 succeeds — the default gateway and routing are fine). Name resolution fails (ping google.com fails — cannot convert the hostname to an IP). Diagnostic steps: nslookup google.com — if this fails, DNS resolution is broken. Check DNS server configuration: ipconfig /all (Windows) or cat /etc/resolv.conf (Linux). Verify the configured DNS server is reachable: ping [DNS server IP]. If the DNS server responds to ping but nslookup fails: the DNS service may be down on that server, or a firewall blocks UDP/TCP 53. nslookup google.com 8.8.8.8 — tests against Google's public DNS to isolate whether it's the specific DNS server or DNS in general. Possible causes: DHCP assigned an incorrect DNS server IP. The DNS server is down or overloaded. A firewall blocks port 53 to the DNS server. The hosts file has a wrong entry for the domain. Fix: correct the DNS server IP in the adapter settings, or correct the DHCP option 6 (DNS server).

prompt: After a user plugs in an unauthorized hub to a switch port configured with port security, the port LED turns amber and the port stops forwarding traffic. What state is the port in and how is it recovered?

options.text: The port is administratively shut down — run 'no shutdown' to recover
The port is in err-disabled state due to a port security violation — re-enable with 'shutdown' then 'no shutdown', or configure automatic err-disable recovery
The port has failed hardware — replace the switch
The switch has detected a spanning tree loop — enable RSTP

explanation: Err-disabled (error-disabled) is a switch port state where the port is automatically disabled due to a security or operational violation. Port security violation: when a device with an unauthorized MAC address is detected (or the maximum MAC count is exceeded), the switch disables the port. The port LED goes amber and it stops forwarding traffic entirely. Other triggers for err-disabled: BPDU Guard violation (STP BPDU received on edge port). Loop Guard. UDLD (Unidirectional Link Detection) failure. Channel misconfig. DHCP snooping violation. How to recover: Manual recovery: interface config → 'shutdown' → 'no shutdown' (port comes back). Auto-recovery: errdisable recovery cause psecure-violation (enables automatic recovery). errdisable recovery interval 300 (recovers after 300 seconds). Diagnose first: show interfaces [interface] status — shows err-disabled. show port-security interface [interface] — shows the violating MAC. Best practice: decide on the violation action when configuring port security: protect (drops frames silently), restrict (drops and logs), shutdown (err-disables the port).

prompt: Users can browse small websites and ping successfully, but connections to specific VPN-protected internal resources fail or hang. A technician suspects an MTU problem. What is the most likely cause and solution?

options.text: The DNS server is returning incorrect IP addresses for internal resources

An MTU mismatch is causing packet fragmentation or the 'Don't Fragment' bit is set and ICMP unreachable messages are blocked — fix by adjusting MSS clamping or reducing the MTU on the tunnel interface
The VPN gateway has run out of licenses
The NIC on the workstation needs a driver update

explanation: MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit): the largest IP packet that a network interface or path can forward. Standard Ethernet MTU: 1500 bytes. VPN tunnels add overhead headers (IPsec: 50-100 bytes, GRE: 24 bytes), effectively reducing the usable MTU. Problem: if a large packet with the DF (Don't Fragment) bit set enters a tunnel with a smaller effective MTU, the router should send an ICMP 'Fragmentation Needed' message back to the sender. Many firewalls block ICMP, so this message never arrives — the sender keeps retransmitting large packets that are silently dropped. Symptom: small packets work (ping, small web pages), large packets fail (file transfers, large web pages, VPN traffic). This is called 'Path MTU Discovery Black Hole.' Solutions: MSS Clamping (TCP Maximum Segment Size): configure the router/firewall to clamp TCP MSS to a lower value (e.g., 1436 for IPsec). This prevents TCP sessions from using oversized packets. Reduce interface MTU on the tunnel endpoint. Allow ICMP type 3 code 4 (Fragmentation Needed) through firewalls to enable proper PMTUD.

prompt: A network has two routers configured with incorrect static routes that point to each other for the same destination. A packet destined for that network is continuously forwarded between the two routers until it is discarded. What prevents packets from looping indefinitely?

options.text: Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) blocks the looping port
The IP TTL (Time to Live) field is decremented by each router — when TTL reaches 0, the packet is discarded and an ICMP Time Exceeded message is sent back
ARP caches prevent duplicate forwarding
BGP detects and breaks routing loops automatically

explanation: TTL (Time to Live) is a field in the IPv4 header (Hop Limit in IPv6) that prevents routing loops from lasting indefinitely. How it works: The sending device sets the initial TTL value (typically 64, 128, or 255 depending on the OS). Each router that forwards the packet decrements the TTL by 1. If the TTL reaches 0, the router discards the packet and sends an ICMP Type 11 'Time Exceeded' message back to the source. This prevents the packet from looping forever, even in a routing loop. TTL values by OS default: Windows: 128. Linux: 64. Cisco IOS: 255. Traceroute uses TTL: sends packets with TTL=1 (discarded at first hop → ICMP response reveals hop 1 IP), then TTL=2, etc. — building a map of the path. Routing loop symptoms: high CPU on affected routers, ICMP Time Exceeded messages flooding, dropped packets to the affected destination, traceroute shows packets bouncing between two or more hops repeatedly. Fix: correct the misconfigured static routes on both routers. Dynamic routing protocols (OSPF, EIGRP) have loop-prevention mechanisms built in.

prompt: A technician troubleshoots a Windows workstation that cannot connect to the network. Running 'ipconfig' shows IP address 169.254.45.22 and subnet mask 255.255.0.0. What does this indicate?

options.text: The workstation has a statically assigned private IP address
The workstation received an APIPA address — DHCP failed, so Windows self-assigned a link-local address
The workstation is configured for IPv6 only
The subnet mask is incorrect — it should be 255.255.255.0

explanation: APIPA (Automatic Private IP Addressing): when a DHCP client cannot reach a DHCP server after repeated attempts, Windows automatically assigns an IP address in the range 169.254.0.1 – 169.254.255.254 with a /16 subnet mask (255.255.0.0). This is a link-local address — devices with APIPA addresses can communicate only with other devices on the same physical segment that also have APIPA addresses (same 169.254.x.x range). They cannot communicate with anything outside the local segment — no internet, no servers on other subnets. Troubleshooting APIPA causes: DHCP server is down or overloaded. The device is on a different VLAN than the DHCP server with no DHCP relay configured. IP helper-address (DHCP relay) is missing on the router interface. Network cable disconnected or switch port down (no DHCP traffic can reach the server). Fix: ipconfig /release && ipconfig /renew — attempt to get a new DHCP lease. If still APIPA, check DHCP server availability, cable, and switch port. On Linux, the equivalent is dhclient or the absence of an IP from 'ip addr show'.

prompt: A user in a conference room at the far corner of the building reports extremely slow Wi-Fi. Their laptop shows connected with 1 bar of signal. What are the MOST likely causes and solutions?

options.text: The AP is overloaded — add more users to fix performance
Physical distance and obstructions (walls, floors) are attenuating the signal — solutions include adding an AP closer to the area or using a wireless range extender
The laptop NIC is broken — replace the laptop
The DNS server is causing the slow connection

explanation: Low wireless signal strength causes: Distance: Wi-Fi signal strength decreases with the square of the distance (inverse square law). The farther from the AP, the weaker the signal. Physical obstructions: Concrete/brick walls: high signal attenuation. Metal surfaces: reflect and block signals. Glass and interior walls: moderate attenuation. Floors/ceilings (between stories): significant attenuation. Interference: other APs on the same channel, microwave ovens (2.4 GHz), Bluetooth, cordless phones (2.4 GHz). Effect of low RSSI: low signal causes the AP and client to negotiate a lower modulation scheme (e.g., drop from 1024-QAM at good signal to BPSK at poor signal), dramatically reducing throughput. Solutions: Deploy additional APs for better coverage (preferred enterprise solution). Wireless range extender/repeater: extends coverage but adds latency and halves throughput on the extended segment. Mesh Wi-Fi: intelligent multi-AP system with seamless roaming. Directional antenna: focuses signal in one direction. Check if the user is associated to the nearest AP (roaming issue — they may be 'stuck' to a distant AP with a strong historical connection). Tools: Wi-Fi analyzer apps, RSSI measurements (good: -50 to -70 dBm; poor: -80 dBm and below).

prompt: A fiber optic link between two switches shows the link LED is not lit on either switch. An OTDR test shows a break 47 meters from the patch panel. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Replace both switches — the hardware has failed
Locate and repair or replace the fiber cable at the break point 47 meters from the patch panel
Replace the transceivers (SFPs) on both switches
Clean the fiber connectors and try again

explanation: OTDR (Optical Time Domain Reflectometer) is the primary diagnostic tool for fiber optic cables. How it works: sends a pulse of light into the fiber and measures reflections over time. Time = distance, allowing it to pinpoint the exact location of faults. What OTDR detects: cable breaks (complete or partial). Connector losses. Splice losses. Bending losses (excessive bends). Contamination (dirty connectors). A clean break at 47 meters: the fiber is physically broken at that distance. Resolution: if the cable is accessible at 47 meters, cut at the break, install new connectors, and splice or re-terminate. If the cable is in conduit and the break point is not accessible, pull a new cable. Fiber troubleshooting order: first — inspect and clean connectors (most fiber issues are dirty connectors). Use a fiber optic cleaning pen or IEC 61300-3-35 compliant cleaning kit. Use a fiber inspection microscope to verify cleanliness. second — use an OTDR to locate faults in the cable. third — use an optical power meter to measure loss. Fiber link budget: maximum allowable attenuation from end to end — compare measured loss against the budget. Never look directly into a live fiber — laser sources can permanently damage eyesight.

prompt: A core router shows 98% CPU utilization during normal business hours. Users experience slow network performance. The router's process list shows 'IP Input' consuming most CPU. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The router's memory is failing — replace hardware
The router is process-switching traffic instead of fast-switching/CEF, or is receiving a high rate of unusual traffic such as a DDoS — check for traffic anomalies and ensure CEF is enabled
The routing table is empty — redistribute routes
An STP loop is causing the router to process excessive broadcast traffic

explanation: High CPU on a router with 'IP Input' process: the 'IP Input' process handles packets that require CPU processing (process switching) rather than hardware/CEF switching. CEF (Cisco Express Forwarding): hardware-accelerated forwarding using the FIB (Forwarding Information Base) and adjacency table. Packets are switched in hardware without CPU involvement — the normal and efficient mode. Causes of high IP Input CPU: CEF disabled: all packets go through the CPU. Run 'show ip cef' to verify CEF is enabled. Unusual traffic: packets with IP options set (Router Alert, Timestamp) must be CPU-processed. TTL expiry responses (traceroute generates many ICMP responses). ICMP flood or DDoS: high volume of traffic forces CPU handling. Incomplete CEF adjacency (ARP not resolved): packets punted to CPU. Management plane traffic: high rate of SSH/SNMP/routing protocol updates. Troubleshooting: show processes cpu sorted — see which processes are high. show ip cef — verify CEF state. show interfaces — check for input errors, drops. show ip traffic — look for unusual traffic types. Mitigation: enable CEF, implement CoPP (Control Plane Policing) to rate-limit traffic destined to the router's CPU.

prompt: A point-to-point wireless bridge is being installed between two buildings 500 meters apart. Which type of antenna should be used on each end to maximize signal strength and minimize interference?

options.text: Omnidirectional antenna — broadcasts equally in all directions for maximum coverage
Directional (Yagi or parabolic dish) antenna — focuses signal in one direction for long-distance point-to-point links
Dipole antenna — standard indoor antenna for general Wi-Fi coverage
Sector antenna — covers a 90-180 degree arc for point-to-multipoint connections

explanation: Wireless antenna types: Omnidirectional: radiates signal equally in all horizontal directions (360°). Gain: 2-9 dBi. Used for: general Wi-Fi coverage areas, indoor APs, client devices. Cannot focus signal — most energy is 'wasted' in unwanted directions for point-to-point. Directional antennas (Yagi, parabolic dish, panel): focuses signal in a narrow beam. Much higher gain: Yagi 10-17 dBi; parabolic dish 20-34 dBi. Used for: long-distance point-to-point links, focused coverage in a specific direction. Parabolic dish: highest gain — used for the longest distances (500m+, several km). Both ends of a point-to-point link need directional antennas aimed precisely at each other. Sector antenna: covers a 60-180° arc with moderate gain (10-19 dBi). Used for: point-to-multipoint — one AP serves multiple clients in a sector. Common for outdoor hotspots, rural wireless ISPs. MIMO (Multiple Input Multiple Output): uses multiple antennas simultaneously for higher throughput. For the 500-meter building-to-building link: directional (parabolic dish or Yagi) antennas aimed at each other on both buildings is the correct choice.

prompt: A newly installed IP camera is not powering on. The camera is connected to a PoE switch and the switch port LED is lit green. What should the technician check first?

options.text: Replace the IP camera — it is defective
Check whether the switch port is PoE-capable and has sufficient PoE budget, and whether the camera's PoE standard matches the switch's capability
Replace the network cable — it must be defective
Reboot the entire network switch to reset all PoE ports

explanation: PoE troubleshooting steps: Verify the switch port is PoE-capable: not all ports on all switches are PoE-enabled. Some switches have a subset of PoE ports. Check the switch documentation or 'show power inline' (Cisco) to see PoE port status. Verify sufficient PoE budget: each switch has a total PoE power budget (e.g., 370W shared among all PoE ports). If all ports are heavily loaded, a new device may not get power even if the port is PoE-capable. 'show power inline' shows per-port allocation and total budget used. Verify PoE standard compatibility: 802.3af (15.4W), 802.3at (30W), 802.3bt (60/100W). If the camera requires 802.3at but the switch only supports 802.3af, the camera won't receive enough power. Check cable quality: PoE requires all 4 pairs (8 wires) for higher-power standards. A damaged cable may pass link negotiation but fail PoE delivery. PoE injector as workaround: an inline PoE injector can be used to power the device from a non-PoE switch port to isolate whether the issue is the switch's PoE capability. Port LED green means the physical link is up — it does not confirm PoE delivery.

prompt: A network administrator notices that syslog timestamps from different network devices differ by several minutes, making it difficult to correlate events during security investigations. Which protocol should be configured to solve this?

options.text: SNMP — polls device status including system time
NTP (Network Time Protocol) — synchronizes clocks across all network devices to a common time source
LLDP — discovers neighboring device information
DNS — resolves hostnames to IP addresses

explanation: NTP (Network Time Protocol) synchronizes the clocks of computers and network devices to a common reference time source. Port: UDP 123. NTP hierarchy (stratum): Stratum 0: reference clock (GPS, atomic clock, radio clock). Stratum 1: NTP servers directly connected to stratum 0 devices. Stratum 2: servers synchronizing from stratum 1. Stratum 15: maximum usable stratum. Stratum 16: unsynchronized. Why accurate time matters: Syslog correlation: when investigating security incidents or outages, log timestamps from multiple devices must be consistent to reconstruct an accurate timeline. Kerberos authentication: requires clocks within 5 minutes. Certificate validity: TLS certificates have validity periods — accurate time is essential for proper validation. Scheduled tasks and billing systems. Configuration on Cisco devices: ntp server [NTP server IP]. Best practice: configure all devices to use internal NTP servers (which sync to public stratum 1/2 servers). Restrict NTP access with NTP authentication (MD5) to prevent NTP amplification attacks.

prompt: A video streaming server needs to send the same live stream to 500 clients simultaneously without sending 500 separate copies of the stream. Which transmission method accomplishes this efficiently?

options.text: Unicast — sends a separate stream to each of the 500 clients
Broadcast — sends to all devices on the network segment
Multicast — sends one stream that is replicated only at network branch points to reach subscribed clients
Anycast — sends to the nearest server in a group

explanation: Transmission types: Unicast: one sender, one receiver. 500 clients = 500 separate streams from the server. Multiplies server bandwidth by 500. Broadcast: one sender, all receivers on the local segment. Cannot cross routers (limited to the broadcast domain). All devices receive the stream whether they want it or not — inefficient and disruptive. Multicast: one sender, multiple subscribed receivers. The server sends ONE stream. Network infrastructure (multicast-enabled routers and switches) replicates the stream only where the network branches toward subscribed clients. Clients subscribe using IGMP (Internet Group Management Protocol). Multicast address range: 224.0.0.0 – 239.255.255.255 (Class D). Protocols: PIM (Protocol Independent Multicast) routes multicast between routers. IGMP snooping: switches use IGMP to forward multicast only to subscribed ports (not flood to all ports). Anycast: one sender, nearest receiver from a group — used for DNS (root servers), CDN edge nodes, BGP anycast services. For live streaming to many clients: multicast is the bandwidth-efficient solution. For a few clients or when multicast isn't supported: CDN (Content Delivery Network) uses unicast to edge servers that distribute the load.

prompt: A network engineer orders SFP modules for a new switch but receives a mix of SX and LX variants. The switch connects to a server 300 meters away over multi-mode fiber. Which SFP variant should be used?

options.text: SX (Short Wavelength) — designed for multi-mode fiber, up to 550 meters at 1 Gbps
LX (Long Wavelength) — designed for single-mode fiber, up to 10 km
ZX (Extended Range) — designed for very long single-mode links
CWDM — wavelength division multiplexing for multiple channels

explanation: SFP (Small Form-factor Pluggable) transceiver variants: SX (Short Wavelength, 850nm): multi-mode fiber. 1000BASE-SX: up to 220 meters on 62.5μm MMF, up to 550 meters on 50μm OM2 MMF. For 10GbE: SFP+ SR — up to 300m on OM3, 400m on OM4. Lower cost. LX (Long Wavelength, 1310nm): single-mode fiber. 1000BASE-LX: up to 10 km on SMF, up to 550 meters on conditioned MMF (with mode conditioning cable). For 10GbE: SFP+ LR — up to 10 km on SMF. ZX (Extended Range, 1550nm): single-mode fiber, up to 70-80 km. For the scenario — 300 meters over multi-mode fiber: SX is correct (MMF + distance within SX range). LX on MMF requires a mode conditioning patch cable for Gigabit and is generally avoided when SX meets the requirement. Additional SFP types: BiDi (bidirectional): uses WDM to send and receive on different wavelengths over one fiber strand. CWDM/DWDM: multiple channels on one fiber using different wavelengths. Always verify compatibility between the SFP vendor and switch manufacturer (some switches require OEM transceivers). Cisco compatible vs. Cisco genuine: third-party SFPs often work but may show 'unsupported' warnings.

prompt: A network administrator enables wireless MAC filtering on a small office AP, allowing only specific MAC addresses to connect. A security auditor says this provides 'security theater' rather than real protection. Why?

options.text: MAC filtering is too complex to implement correctly
Attackers can use a wireless adapter to capture allowed MAC addresses from the air and spoof them trivially, bypassing MAC filtering with minimal effort
MAC filtering only works on wired networks, not wireless
MAC filtering requires a RADIUS server to function

explanation: MAC filtering limitations: MAC addresses are transmitted in plaintext in every wireless frame — even before association. Any attacker with a wireless adapter in monitor mode (using tools like airodump-ng) can passively capture the MAC addresses of all devices communicating with the AP. The attacker then configures their wireless adapter to spoof an allowed MAC address (macchanger, ifconfig hw ether). The attacker is now indistinguishable from an authorized device from the AP's perspective. MAC spoofing takes less than a minute and requires no special skills with readily available tools. Why MAC filtering is still used (despite limitations): Adds a minor speed bump — script kiddies may be deterred. Combined with other controls, provides defense in depth. Useful as an additional layer, not a primary control. Real wireless security: WPA3-Enterprise with 802.1X and certificate-based authentication (EAP-TLS) is the only robust wireless security mechanism — even if an attacker spoofs a MAC, they still need valid credentials/certificates to complete 802.1X authentication. WPA2/3-Personal with strong passphrase: much more effective than MAC filtering. The auditor's 'security theater' comment is accurate — MAC filtering alone provides negligible real security.

prompt: A network team struggles with IP address conflicts because different administrators manually assign static IPs from a spreadsheet. Two servers end up with the same IP address. What system should be implemented to prevent this?

options.text: Configure all servers with DHCP instead of static IPs
Implement an IPAM (IP Address Management) system to centrally track, manage, and allocate IP addresses across the entire network
Disable ARP on all switches to prevent IP conflicts
Increase the subnet size to provide more IP addresses

explanation: IPAM (IP Address Management) centralizes the management, tracking, and allocation of IP addresses across an organization. Core IPAM functions: IP address inventory: tracks which IP addresses are assigned, to which devices, and which are available. Conflict detection: identifies duplicate IP assignments before they cause outages. DNS and DHCP integration (DDI — DNS, DHCP, IPAM): automatically updates DNS when IP assignments change; manages DHCP scopes. Subnet management: tracks subnet utilization, plans new subnets, documents IP schemas. Historical tracking: logs when an IP was assigned, to which device, and for how long. Reporting and alerting: warns when subnets approach full capacity. Commercial IPAM solutions: SolarWinds IPAM, Infoblox, BlueCat, Men&Mice. Open source: phpIPAM, NetBox. Integrated solutions: Microsoft DHCP/DNS server provides basic IPAM functionality in Windows Server. The core problem described (spreadsheet-based static IP tracking with no conflict prevention): IPAM solves this through centralized tracking with built-in conflict detection. For very small networks: a simple spreadsheet with strict process controls can work, but IPAM is the scalable solution.

prompt: A large enterprise network has 500 routers in a single OSPF area. Network engineers notice very slow convergence after topology changes and high CPU usage on all routers from LSA flooding. What OSPF design change addresses this?

options.text: Replace OSPF with RIP — simpler protocol with less overhead
Implement OSPF area design: divide routers into multiple areas connected via Area 0 (backbone), reducing LSA flooding to within each area
Increase router CPU and RAM to handle more LSA processing
Enable OSPF stub areas only — this solves all scalability issues

explanation: OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) area design: In a single large OSPF area, every topology change causes an LSA (Link State Advertisement) flood to ALL routers in the area. Every router must rerun the Dijkstra SPF algorithm after each change. In large areas: massive LSA storms, high CPU, slow convergence, large LSDB (Link State Database). OSPF multi-area design: Area 0 (Backbone): all areas must connect to Area 0. ABRs (Area Border Routers) connect non-backbone areas to Area 0. Benefits: LSA flooding is contained within each area — a change in Area 1 does not flood to Area 2. Smaller LSDB per router — less memory and CPU needed. Faster convergence within each area. ABRs summarize routes between areas — reduces routing table size. Special area types: Stub area: no external routes (Type 5 LSAs) allowed — routers use a default route instead. Totally stubby (Cisco): only intra-area and default routes. NSSA (Not-So-Stubby Area): allows limited external routes via Type 7 LSAs. Recommendation for 500 routers: design with multiple areas of 50-100 routers each, all connecting to a well-connected Area 0 backbone with redundant ABRs.

prompt: A network analyzer captures an Ethernet frame with EtherType value 0x0800. What does this indicate about the frame's payload?

options.text: The frame carries an ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) packet
The frame carries an IPv4 packet
The frame carries an IPv6 packet
The frame carries a VLAN tag (802.1Q)

explanation: EtherType is a 2-byte field in the Ethernet frame header that identifies the protocol encapsulated in the payload. Common EtherType values: 0x0800: IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4). 0x0806: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol). 0x86DD: IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6). 0x8100: IEEE 802.1Q VLAN tagging. 0x8847: MPLS unicast. 0x8848: MPLS multicast. 0x88CC: LLDP (Link Layer Discovery Protocol). 0x0842: Wake-on-LAN. Ethernet frame structure: Preamble (7 bytes) + SFD (1 byte) — used for clock synchronization and frame delineation. Destination MAC (6 bytes). Source MAC (6 bytes). EtherType/Length (2 bytes) — if ≥ 0x0600, it's an EtherType; if < 0x0600, it's the payload length (original IEEE 802.3). Payload: 46 to 1500 bytes (minimum 46 ensures detectable collisions; maximum 1500 is standard MTU). FCS (Frame Check Sequence, 4 bytes) — CRC error detection. Jumbo frames: non-standard extended MTU (typically 9000 bytes) — used in storage networks, requires support on all devices in the path.

prompt: A data center technician notices an unfamiliar USB device plugged into a switch's console port in an unlocked rack. What physical security controls should be in place to prevent this?

options.text: Firewall rules to block USB traffic
Locked equipment racks, physical access control (badge/PIN/biometric) to the data center, cable locks on console ports, and a visitor escort policy
VLAN segmentation to isolate console traffic
Enabling SSH instead of console access eliminates the risk

explanation: Physical security for network infrastructure: Locked equipment racks: cabinets with keyed or card-controlled locks prevent unauthorized access to equipment. Different lock cylinders for different access levels. Physical access control to the data center: badge readers (RFID/smart card), PIN pads, biometric scanners (fingerprint, iris). Two-factor physical access: badge + PIN. Mantrap/airlock: prevents tailgating. Visitor management: sign in/out log, escort policy — visitors never left alone in the data center. Console port security: blank/dummy plugs in unused console ports. Console port access often requires physical presence — a critical backdoor if unsecured. USB port blockers: physically block USB ports on servers and switches to prevent unauthorized device insertion. Cable management: proper cable management makes it obvious when something is added or changed. Surveillance cameras: record all physical access for audit and incident investigation. Why physical security is paramount: the most sophisticated logical security can be bypassed if an attacker has physical access to the hardware. Physical access to a console port = complete device control regardless of network-level authentication.

prompt: A technician uses Wireshark to capture traffic on a network segment. They see thousands of ARP requests per second from a single MAC address asking 'Who has [various IPs]?' What does this pattern indicate?

options.text: Normal network behavior — ARP is always frequent
An ARP scan or network reconnaissance — a device is actively scanning the subnet to discover live hosts
A failing NIC — hardware errors generate ARP flood
DNS is down and devices are falling back to ARP for name resolution

explanation: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) scanning: normal ARP behavior — a device sends an ARP request only when it needs the MAC address for a specific IP it wants to communicate with. Typical rate: a few ARP requests per minute per device. Abnormal ARP pattern (as described — thousands per second, many different IPs): this is an ARP sweep/scan — a tool (like Nmap with -sn option, or arp-scan) is systematically sending ARP requests to every IP in the subnet to discover which hosts are alive. Why ARP-based discovery: ARP requests cannot be blocked by host-based firewalls (they operate at Layer 2 below the IP stack). Even devices blocking ICMP (ping) will respond to ARP requests, making ARP scanning more comprehensive than ICMP pings on the local subnet. Security implications: this indicates active reconnaissance — either an authorized network administrator running an asset discovery scan, OR an attacker (insider or compromised device) mapping the network before lateral movement. Investigate: identify the source MAC and track it to a switch port. Determine whether the scan is authorized. Response: if unauthorized, isolate the device, investigate for compromise. IDS systems flag excessive ARP traffic as a reconnaissance indicator.
